svg.text: Two doors to the database, and three layers of key
withOrg(orgId, fn) — the door for everything with a session behind it
Opens a transaction, drops to the kaddiya_app role (NOBYPASSRLS), pins
app.org_id. Every tenant policy reads that setting, so a query in here
cannot reach another org's rows even if the SQL forgets its WHERE clause.
The setting is absent outside this door, and the policy raises rather than
returning empty — a stray query errors instead of leaking.
system(fn) — only before a tenant is known
Which org owns this hostname? Which session does this cookie name?
Which org does this MCP bearer belong to? Creating an org.
Four modules may call it: db, tenancy, sessions, billing.
A test greps the whole server for system( and fails the build if it
appears anywhere else.
FORCE row-level security — tenant rows
conversations · notebook_entries · audit_events · usage_events · members
Subject to the policy even for the table owner. On audit_events the app
role additionally has UPDATE and DELETE revoked: the console can write its
own history and never rewrite it.
ENABLE row-level security — directory rows
orgs · instances · instance_aliases · sessions · oauth_states · mcp_tokens
The app role is confined to its org by the same policy; the owner role can
resolve a hostname, a cookie or a bearer before any org is known — which is
the one thing it exists to do.
Three keys, none of which the database holds
A master key (env var, file, or KMS) wraps a per-org data key, which seals tenant content with AAD org_id:column.
Ciphertext written for one org cannot be opened in another's request, and a blob from one column cannot be read as another.
ServiceNow tokens are sealed separately, under HKDF(the credential that fetched them) — so the org key alone opens nothing.
